passage:
Tejas, put the phone face down for a minute and listen to your Ganga Masi.
When I was sixteen, there was a boy called Sunil. We had those small phones then, only texts. If he didn't reply in ten minutes, my stomach dropped. I'd check the phone under my pillow, in the bathroom, during prayers. Once, when he went quiet for an evening, I told him another boy had walked me home. It wasn't even true. I just wanted him to feel as scared as I did.
He was hurt, and we nearly broke up.
That night I made myself a small rule. When the dread came, I would write it in my diary first, then call my friend Lata or walk round the colony. Only after that could I text him.
It was hard. Some nights I wrote three pages. But the texts I sent after were kinder, and so was I.

qa.q: Where did young Ganga check her phone?
qa.a: Under her pillow, in the bathroom and during prayers.

qa.q: How did young Ganga feel when Sunil didn't reply?
qa.a: She felt dread and fear; her stomach dropped if he didn't reply in ten minutes, and she wanted him to feel as scared as she did.

qa.q: What choice did young Ganga make after nearly breaking up, and why did it help?
qa.a: She decided to write in her diary, call Lata or walk before texting, which calmed the dread so her texts were kinder.

qa.q: How was Sunil affected when she invented the story about another boy?
qa.a: He was hurt by it, and they nearly broke up, because the jealousy test made him doubt her.

grounding: Shows an aunt recalling a teenage romance where she checked for replies, felt dread and tested with jealousy, then learned to soothe herself first.

passage:
Monday: Dolma hadn't replied since lunch. Ritu sent "?" then "hello??" then "are you mad at me". Her chest was tight all evening, and she couldn't focus on anything.
Thursday: Dolma was quiet again. Ritu's thumb hovered over a fourth message. She put the phone down and said out loud, "I'm scared she's pulling away." Then she typed one text: "Hey, I get worried when things go quiet. Can you tell me if we're okay?" Dolma replied an hour later: "We're fine!! Just exams."
Two weeks later: Ritu had joined the school pottery club on Wednesdays and started messaging Sonam from the club too. When Dolma went quiet on Sunday, Ritu noticed the worry, and went back to shaping her lopsided bowl.

qa.q: What club did Ritu join?
qa.a: The school pottery club on Wednesdays.

qa.q: What was Ritu afraid of on Thursday?
qa.a: She was scared that Dolma was pulling away from her, and she named that fear out loud before texting.

qa.q: Which step on Thursday worked, and why?
qa.a: Ritu paused instead of sending a fourth message, named the fear, and asked directly whether they were okay, which got a clear answer.

qa.q: What might Monday's messages have been like for Dolma?
qa.a: Dolma, busy with exams, might have felt pressured or confused by several worried texts in a row.

grounding: Shows a teen learning to pause before another text, name her fear, ask directly, and build other friendships and interests.

subtype: Fear of abandonment in adult love [Actor]
passage:
"You said 'fine' with a full stop," Arohi said, standing in the doorway of the flat. "That means you're annoyed with me."
Francis looked up from the laptop. "It means I'm finishing a report."
"You always do this. You pull away and then you'll just leave one day."
"Arohi—"
"Forget it!" She slammed the bedroom door.
Twenty minutes later she opened it, eyes red. "I'm sorry. That was horrible of me."
"It was a lot," Francis said quietly. "What happened?"
"When you went short, I felt like you were already gone. It's an old fear. It isn't about the full stop."
"Thank you for telling me. I'm not going anywhere. Next time, can you ask me first, before the door?"
Arohi nodded, ashamed and a little relieved. "I'll try. Ask first."

qa.q: What was Francis doing when Arohi came to the doorway?
qa.a: Francis was finishing a report on the laptop.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel after slamming the door?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, calling it horrible, and also a little relieved once she explained her fear of being left.

qa.q: What did Francis ask Arohi to try next time?
qa.a: To ask first, before slamming the door, so the fear can be checked instead of acted on.

qa.q: How might Francis feel when Arohi says "you'll just leave one day"?
qa.a: Francis may feel hurt and accused over a report and a full stop, yet stays calm and reassures her once she explains.

grounding: Shows a young adult who reads a short reply as rejection, lashes out, then feels shame and names her fear of being left.

passage:
Counsellor's session note, Tanuja and Aparna, week three.
Tanuja said she feels "watched". Aparna asks where she is several times a day and gets upset if a reply takes long. Tanuja admitted she has started leaving her phone in her bag on purpose. Aparna's eyes filled: "That's exactly when I feel you're leaving."
I pointed out the loop gently: the more one asks, the more the other hides, and the hiding feeds the fear.
Tanuja said, "I love her. I just can't prove it every hour." She looked worn out.
What we did next: Tanuja chose what she can keep up warmly: a message when she leaves the office and a call at lunch. She also named a limit: no tracking her location. Aparna agreed to note her worry in a notebook before messaging. We will review in two weeks.

qa.q: What limit did Tanuja name?
qa.a: No tracking her location.

qa.q: How was Tanuja feeling in the session?
qa.a: She felt watched and worn out, loving Aparna but unable to prove it every hour.

qa.q: Why is Tanuja's plan better than giving in or hiding the phone?
qa.a: A message when she leaves office and a call at lunch give warm consistency, while the no-tracking limit protects her, so neither of them feeds the loop.

qa.q: How does Tanuja's hidden phone look from Aparna's side?
qa.a: To Aparna, it is exactly when she feels Tanuja is leaving, so the withdrawal confirms her fear.

grounding: Shows a partner who feels watched and pulls away, and how warm consistency plus a clear limit helps more than giving in or withdrawing.

subtype: Toddler who does not seek comfort [Actor]
passage:
At the village anganwadi, Ira's mother waved and left for the fields. Ira didn't look up. She stacked steel cups alone in the corner.
Later she tripped on the step and scraped her hand. She turned her face to the wall, lips pressed, and didn't cry.
Jyoti, the anganwadi worker, sat down near her, not too close, and held out a wet cloth. After a long moment, Ira let her wipe the scrape.

qa.q: What did Ira stack in the corner?
qa.a: Steel cups.

qa.q: How might Ira have been feeling when she scraped her hand?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and upset, but she turned to the wall with her lips pressed instead of crying or asking for help.

qa.q: Why was Jyoti's approach wise?
qa.a: She came near without crowding Ira and simply offered the cloth, showing that comfort is available without forcing it.

qa.q: How might Jyoti see Ira's calm?
qa.a: Jyoti seems to sense the calm may hide stress, since she still sits near Ira and offers care even though Ira did not cry.

grounding: Shows a toddler who seems unbothered at parting and turns away when hurt, and a carer who offers comfort gently.

passage:
Rain was drumming on the roof and the school van was honking outside. "Lakshmi, let me do the buckle," Amma said.
"No! I do it." Lakshmi's fingers slipped on the wet strap.
The van honked again. Amma reached down. Lakshmi pulled her foot away, tried again and fell on her bottom.
Her chin shook, but she turned her face to the door. Amma sat beside her. "That was frustrating." She held her arms open. Lakshmi shook her head and stayed where she was.
"Okay. I'll be here." Amma did the buckle, then waited. Just before running to the van, Lakshmi leaned her head on Amma's arm for one second.

qa.q: What was drumming on the roof?
qa.a: Rain.

qa.q: How was Lakshmi feeling when she fell?
qa.a: She was upset and frustrated; her chin shook, but she hid it by turning her face to the door.

qa.q: What did Amma do that respected Lakshmi and still offered closeness?
qa.a: Amma named the frustration, opened her arms without forcing a hug, and said "I'll be here," then waited.

qa.q: What might Amma feel when Lakshmi refuses her hug?
qa.a: Amma may feel a little sad or shut out, yet she stays patient, and the one-second lean shows her waiting mattered.

grounding: Shows a young child insisting on doing things alone and pulling away from hugs when upset, perhaps guarding against disappointment.

passage:
Preeti, beta, you say you don't care that they didn't invite you. I said that too, once. Listen to your Noor Nani.
When I was ten, the girls in my class made a skipping group and never asked me. I told everyone, "Who cares? I like carrom better," and played carrom alone for hours. At home, tears were for babies.
Then a new teacher came, Miss D'Souza. She never said, "Tell me your problems." She just sat down at my carrom board one lunch and played, and came back the next week, and the next.
One day she said, "If you ever want to talk, I'm here. If not, we'll just play." For a month I said nothing. Then one afternoon I told her about the skipping group, and I cried on the board.

qa.q: What game did young Noor play alone?
qa.a: Carrom.

qa.q: How did young Noor feel about being left out, beneath what she said?
qa.a: She said "Who cares?" but was really hurt and lonely, which came out when she finally cried telling Miss D'Souza.

qa.q: What choice did Miss D'Souza make that let young Noor open up?
qa.a: She kept showing up to play without asking questions, then offered to listen with no pressure, leaving the choice to Noor.

qa.q: How might Miss D'Souza have felt waiting a month for Noor to talk?
qa.a: She probably needed patience and hope, choosing to trust that steady games would help rather than pushing.

grounding: Shows a grandmother recalling how, as a child who claimed not to care about being left out, a teacher's pressure-free invitations let her feelings come out.

passage:
Week one: Deepika Ma'am noticed that Lalit never raised his hand for help, even when his sums were wrong. When Arun tore his notebook, Lalit shrugged and kept writing. She wondered what the shrug was holding in.
Week three: Instead of calling him to her desk, she crouched by his bench. "Want to try the next one with me, or on your own first?" He chose "own first". She said, "I'll be at the window if you want me."
Week six: During a thunderstorm, the class got noisy. Lalit walked over to the window and stood next to her, not speaking. After a minute he said, "Ma'am, I didn't get question four." She smiled, careful not to make a fuss, and pulled up a chair.

qa.q: What did Arun do to Lalit's notebook?
qa.a: Arun tore his notebook.

qa.q: What was Deepika Ma'am feeling about Lalit's shrug in week one?
qa.a: She felt concerned and curious about what the shrug was holding in, since he never asked for help.

qa.q: Which of Deepika Ma'am's steps helped Lalit come closer?
qa.a: Giving him a choice instead of a demand and saying she would be at the window, so he knew where help was without pressure.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Lalit to ask about question four?
qa.a: It was probably a big, slightly nervous step for Lalit, easier because she stayed calm and didn't make a fuss.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a self-contained child and, over weeks, using quiet check-ins, choices and steady availability until he comes closer.

passage:
Nirmala and Jahnavi had walked to the government school together for a year, sharing tamarind and gossip. Then one evening by the tube well, Jahnavi cried and told her about the fights at home. "Now you tell me something real," she said. "What's hard for you?"
Nirmala's throat went tight. "Nothing. I'm fine." The next morning she left early and took the long road past the rice mill, alone.
For three days she avoided Jahnavi. It felt safer, and also strangely empty.
On the fourth day, Jahnavi was waiting at the crossroads. Nirmala stopped. She picked one small true thing. "I get scared about Class 10 results. My father keeps talking about them."
Jahnavi just nodded and handed her a piece of tamarind. They walked on. Nirmala's shoulders slowly came down.

qa.q: Where did Jahnavi tell Nirmala about the fights at home?
qa.a: By the tube well.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel when Jahnavi asked her to share something real?
qa.a: She felt tense and threatened; her throat went tight, and later avoiding Jahnavi felt safer but also strangely empty.

qa.q: What small step did Nirmala take toward being open?
qa.a: She picked one small true thing to share, her worry about Class 10 results, instead of everything at once.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi have felt during the three days Nirmala avoided her?
qa.a: Jahnavi may have felt hurt or confused after opening up, yet she still waited at the crossroads.

grounding: Shows a teen who pulls back when a friendship turns emotional and then practises vulnerability with one small share.
